name: National Assembly
tagline: Where the nation's laws are made
description: The National Assembly is Nigeria's federal law-making body. It has two chambers, and both must agree before a bill can become law: the Senate, where every state has equal representation, and the House of Representatives, where seats are shared according to population. Beyond making laws, it approves how public money is spent and questions the Executive on how that money is used.

keyFacts.label: Chambers
keyFacts.value: Senate + House of Representatives

keyFacts.label: Senate
keyFacts.value: 109 senators — three per state, plus one for the FCT

keyFacts.label: House of Representatives
keyFacts.value: 360 members, elected from federal constituencies

keyFacts.label: Term
keyFacts.value: 4 years, with no limit on how many times a member may be re-elected

keyFacts.label: Led by
keyFacts.value: President of the Senate; Speaker of the House of Representatives

keyFacts.label: Current leadership
keyFacts.value: Godswill Akpabio, President of the Senate; Tajudeen Abbas, Speaker of the House of Representatives

keyFacts.label: Core function
keyFacts.value: Makes federal laws, approves the budget, checks the Executive

keyFacts.label: Located
keyFacts.value: Three Arms Zone, Abuja

whyItMatters: Almost every national rule that shapes daily life begins here — taxes, education policy, road funding, the security budget. Your senator and your representative are the two people in Abuja you elected directly to speak for your area, and the ones you can hold to account at the next election.
checksOnIt: A bill the Assembly passes is not yet law: it needs the President's assent, and if assent is withheld the Assembly must pass it again by a two-thirds majority in each chamber. Whatever it does pass can still be struck down by the courts if it conflicts with the Constitution.
didYouKnow: The two chambers are known by their colours. The Senate sits in the Red Chamber and the House of Representatives in the Green Chamber, and both are served by a central atrium beneath the famous green dome.
inYourDailyLife: When the Assembly passes the annual budget, it decides how much goes to the federal roads, hospitals and schools in your state — and it makes the law governing how money from the Federation Account is shared with your State and your Local Government.

hotspots.label: The Senate (Red Chamber)
hotspots.blurb: 109 senators. Every state sends three, regardless of size, so a small state has the same voice here as a large one. The Red Chamber is inside the central building, on the eastern side of the atrium.

hotspots.label: House of Representatives (Green Chamber)
hotspots.blurb: 360 members elected from federal constituencies drawn by population, so busier areas hold more seats. The Green Chamber is in the same central building, on the western side of the atrium.

hotspots.label: The Green Dome
hotspots.blurb: The landmark of the complex. Beneath it runs the central atrium that both chambers open onto — which is why the whole National Assembly is pictured by this one roof.

hotspots.label: The wing buildings
hotspots.blurb: Two five-storey wings flank the domed building, added years after it, giving the Senate and the House the offices and workrooms the chambers themselves have no space for.

modelNote: The model is a schematic, not a floor plan. Markers point at the part of the building that houses each thing, not its exact room.

name: Aso Rock Villa
tagline: Where the nation's laws are carried out
description: Aso Rock Villa is the official residence and office of the President, and the seat of the Executive arm. The Executive's job is to carry out the laws the National Assembly passes: running the ministries, commanding the armed forces, conducting relations with other countries and proposing the annual budget. The President is both Head of State and Head of Government, and is elected directly by voters across the whole country.

keyFacts.label: Head of the Executive
keyFacts.value: The President — Head of State, Head of Government and Commander-in-Chief

keyFacts.label: Deputy
keyFacts.value: The Vice President

keyFacts.label: Term
keyFacts.value: 4 years, renewable once — a maximum of two terms

keyFacts.label: Cabinet
keyFacts.value: The Federal Executive Council, made up of ministers

keyFacts.label: Ministers
keyFacts.value: At least one from every state, appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate

keyFacts.label: Current President
keyFacts.value: Bola Ahmed Tinubu

keyFacts.label: Core function
keyFacts.value: Implements the laws, runs the ministries, proposes the budget

keyFacts.label: Located
keyFacts.value: Three Arms Zone, Abuja

whyItMatters: The Executive is the arm you meet most often, even if you never see the President. Every ministry, agency, police officer and passport office acts on its authority. It also proposes the budget, so its priorities shape what actually gets funded.
checksOnIt: The President cannot spend money the National Assembly has not appropriated, and cannot seat a minister the Senate has not confirmed. The courts can rule an executive action unlawful. And a President can be removed for gross misconduct — but only through a chain that runs across all three arms: two-thirds of each chamber must vote to investigate, a seven-member panel appointed by the Chief Justice must find the allegation proved, and two-thirds of each chamber must then vote to remove.
didYouKnow: The Villa takes its name from Aso Rock, the granite monolith rising directly behind it — one of the few seats of government in the world identified by a natural landmark rather than by the building itself.
inYourDailyLife: Your passport, your national identity number, the body that approves the medicines in your pharmacy, the duty charged on goods brought into the country — all sit with federal ministries and agencies that answer to the Presidency.

hotspots.label: The President's Office
hotspots.blurb: Where the President works, and where a bill arrives from the National Assembly to be assented to — or not.

hotspots.label: Council Chamber
hotspots.blurb: Where the Federal Executive Council — the President, Vice President and ministers — meets to take decisions together.

hotspots.label: Aso Rock
hotspots.blurb: The granite monolith behind the Villa that gives the complex its name.

hotspots.label: The Forecourt
hotspots.blurb: Where visiting heads of state are formally received, and where national ceremonies are held.

modelNote: The model is a schematic, not a floor plan. Markers point at the part of the building that houses each thing, not its exact room.

name: Supreme Court of Nigeria
tagline: Where the law has the final word
description: The Supreme Court is the highest court in Nigeria. It hears appeals from the Court of Appeal and its decisions are final — no other court can overturn them. It also settles disputes between the Federal Government and a state, or between two states, and it has the last word on what the Constitution means. Its role is to check both the Legislature and the Executive by ruling on whether what they have done is lawful.

keyFacts.label: Highest court
keyFacts.value: Its decisions are final and bind every other court

keyFacts.label: Composition
keyFacts.value: The Chief Justice of Nigeria and up to 21 other Justices

keyFacts.label: Appointed by
keyFacts.value: The President, on the recommendation of the National Judicial Council, subject to Senate confirmation

keyFacts.label: Security of tenure
keyFacts.value: A Justice cannot be dismissed at will, and only for inability to do the job, misconduct or breach of the Code of Conduct. Removing the Chief Justice takes an address supported by two-thirds of the Senate; any other Justice goes on the recommendation of the National Judicial Council.

keyFacts.label: Retirement age
keyFacts.value: A Justice may retire at 65 and must leave office at 70

keyFacts.label: Sits in panels
keyFacts.value: Never the whole court at once — no fewer than five Justices, and seven where it interprets the Constitution, rules on fundamental rights, or hears a case in its original jurisdiction

keyFacts.label: Original jurisdiction
keyFacts.value: Disputes between the Federation and a state, or between states

keyFacts.label: Current Chief Justice
keyFacts.value: Honourable Justice Kudirat Motonmori Olatokunbo Kekere-Ekun, GCON

keyFacts.label: Located
keyFacts.value: Three Arms Zone, Abuja

whyItMatters: This is where an ordinary citizen can, in principle, defeat the government. If a law or an official action breaches your constitutional rights, this is the court that can strike it down — and neither the President nor the National Assembly can overrule it.
checksOnIt: The court cannot act on its own initiative — it decides only the cases actually brought before it, and decides them on the law rather than on what it thinks best. Its Justices are appointed by the President on the recommendation of the National Judicial Council and confirmed by the Senate, and the National Assembly can rewrite the ordinary law the court applies, though changing the Constitution itself takes a formal amendment. The trade is deliberate: in exchange, a Justice cannot be sacked for a ruling the government dislikes.
didYouKnow: Nigeria's highest court only became truly final in 1963. Before then, cases could still be appealed beyond Nigeria to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London.
inYourDailyLife: Its rulings settle what the rules actually mean — who legitimately holds an office after a disputed election, whether a tax or a levy was lawfully imposed, and how far the police may go. Every lower court that hears an ordinary case is bound by what it decides.

hotspots.label: The courtroom
hotspots.blurb: Where the Justices sit as a panel to hear appeals. No witnesses and no new evidence — only argument about what the law means. Each Justice may give their own reasons, and the view of the majority binds every other court.

hotspots.label: The Coat of Arms
hotspots.blurb: Mounted above the entrance, marking the court as an institution of the Federal Republic rather than of any government of the day.

hotspots.label: Forecourt and Steps
hotspots.blurb: The public approach to the court — the point at which a dispute stops being political and becomes a legal question.

name: LGA Secretariat
tagline: The tier of government closest to you

name: INEC
description: The Independent National Electoral Commission runs Nigeria's federal and state elections. It registers voters and political parties, draws the constituencies, and conducts the polls for President, Governors, the National Assembly and the State Houses of Assembly. It belongs to none of the three arms: the Constitution sets it up as a commission of its own, so that the people competing for power are not the ones counting the votes.

keyFacts.label: Established by
keyFacts.value: The Constitution, which lists it among the federal bodies that must exist

keyFacts.label: Composition
keyFacts.value: A Chairman, who is the Chief Electoral Commissioner, and twelve National Electoral Commissioners

keyFacts.label: Who may serve
keyFacts.value: Only someone non-partisan and of unquestionable integrity; the Chairman must be at least 40 and a Commissioner at least 35

keyFacts.label: Appointed by
keyFacts.value: The President, after consulting the Council of State, subject to confirmation by the Senate

keyFacts.label: Term
keyFacts.value: Five years from the date of appointment

keyFacts.label: Removal
keyFacts.value: Only by the President acting on an address supported by two-thirds of the Senate, and only for inability to do the job or for misconduct

keyFacts.label: Runs elections for
keyFacts.value: President and Vice-President, Governors and Deputy Governors, the Senate, the House of Representatives and every State House of Assembly

keyFacts.label: Does not run
keyFacts.value: Local government elections, which belong to each state's own State Independent Electoral Commission

keyFacts.label: In every state
keyFacts.value: A Resident Electoral Commissioner for each state and for the Federal Capital Territory, appointed by the President subject to confirmation by the Senate

keyFacts.label: Draws the map
keyFacts.value: Divides each state into three Senatorial districts and the country into 360 Federal constituencies, and reviews the division at intervals of not less than ten years

keyFacts.label: Current Chairman
keyFacts.value: Professor Joash Amupitan, SAN

keyFacts.label: Located
keyFacts.value: Plot 436 Zambezi Crescent, Maitama, Abuja

whyItMatters: Every elected office in the first two tiers of government, from the President to a member of a State House of Assembly, is filled by an election this body runs. If its count is not believed, nothing that comes out of the buildings in the Three Arms Zone is either.
checksOnIt: Its members are chosen by the President and confirmed by the Senate, the same politicians whose elections it goes on to run. The Constitution answers that by making them hard to get rid of: removal takes an address backed by two-thirds of the Senate, and only for inability or misconduct. The Commission registers and monitors the parties, but the law it applies is made by the National Assembly, and a result it declares can be challenged before an election tribunal or a court.
didYouKnow: Two numbers on the electoral map are not INEC's to change. The Constitution fixes three Senatorial districts for every state, whatever its size, and 360 Federal constituencies for the whole country. The Commission's job is only to draw the lines.
inYourDailyLife: Your voter's card comes from here. So does the register your name has to be on, the polling unit you are assigned to, and the list of parties allowed on the ballot paper you are handed.

hotspots.label: The Commission
hotspots.blurb: A Chairman and twelve National Electoral Commissioners take the Commission's decisions together. Each is appointed for five years and can be removed only on an address supported by two-thirds of the Senate.

hotspots.label: The register of voters
hotspots.blurb: Nobody votes whose name is not on it. Registering everyone qualified to vote, and keeping that register up to date for every election, is one of the powers the Constitution gives the Commission by name.

hotspots.label: The gate on Zambezi Crescent
hotspots.blurb: The headquarters stands in Maitama, not in the Three Arms Zone. The body that fills the seats in the National Assembly and the Villa is housed apart from both.

modelNote: The model is a schematic of the tower, the lower wing in front of it, the gate and the fence as they look from the street. A second, lower block on the site is left out because no photograph shows where it stands, and so is the new annex, which is still being built.
